comment: Brian (ElevenLabs) VO for WorldCup26 Bonus — Luis Díaz (300s drama film). VERIFIED facts (cite in README): Born 13 Jan 1997 in Barrancas, La Guajira — home of the indigenous WAYUU people, one of Colombia's poorest regions (Wayuu under-5 malnutrition death rate ~6x the national rate). Luis grew up thin/underweight and was repeatedly OVERLOOKED for his size. His father Luis Manuel was an amateur player who ran a small neighbourhood football academy and sold 'friche' (a traditional Wayuu dish) to fund Luis's trips to trials. 2015: Colombia's first indigenous football tournament — Carlos Valderrama spotted him and picked him for the Copa América de Pueblos Indígenas in Chile; that changed everything. Rise: Junior Barranquilla → Porto → Liverpool (now Bayern Munich). 28 Oct 2023: his father was KIDNAPPED by the ELN armed group in Barrancas (his mother Cilenis was rescued by police within hours). Days later Luis scored a 95th-minute equaliser vs Luton and lifted his shirt: 'LIBERTAD PARA PAPÁ' (Freedom for dad). After ~12 days the ELN — admitting it was a mistake — released his father. Today he is a Colombian idol. SENSITIVITY: frame the kidnapping respectfully — a son's love and a family's resilience; NO graphic detail, no politics, do not glorify the group. Brian narrator. NO subtitles on screen. Soccer only. Lines short.

lines.text: Ninety-fifth minute. He scores. And instead of celebrating, he lifts his shirt — and shows the world a desperate, secret message.
Four words, hidden against his heart. A plea. Because somewhere far away, the most important man in his life had vanished. This is the story of Luis Díaz — and the longest twelve days of his life.
To understand that night, you have to go back to the desert. To one of the poorest corners of Colombia.
Barrancas. La Guajira. The land of the Wayuu people — a place of sun, dust, and a hunger the rest of the world rarely sees.
Here, children grow up thirsty. In this community, far too many do not grow up at all.
And here, a small, skinny boy fell in love with a ball — even as the world kept telling him he was too frail to matter.
Scouts looked at him and saw a child who was underfed. Underweight. Too small. Again and again, they passed him by.
But one man never doubted him. His father, Luis Manuel — once a player himself — who ran a tiny football school in the dust.
To pay for his son's journeys to trials, his father sold friche — a traditional Wayuu dish — plate by plate, mile by mile.
Two men against the desert. A father's faith, and a boy who refused to believe he was too small for a big dream.
Then, in twenty fifteen, fate finally knocked. Colombia held its first ever tournament for indigenous players.
And watching from the stands was a legend — the great Carlos Valderrama, the golden mane of Colombian football.
He saw the skinny kid from La Guajira tear the game apart. Pace. Courage. Magic. And he chose him.
That was the door. Junior of Barranquilla. Then Porto, in Europe. And then — Liverpool. Anfield. The biggest stage of all.
The boy they said was too small was now terrorising the finest defenders on Earth. The dream had come true.
And then — the phone call that every child of La Guajira fears.
The twenty-eighth of October, twenty twenty-three. Back home in Barrancas, armed men seize his mother... and his father.
His mother is found within hours. But his father — the man who sold friche for his dream — disappears into the mountains.
Imagine it. The world at your feet... and the one who put you there, simply gone. Nobody knows where. Nobody knows if he is alive.
Days pass. Then a week. Still nothing. And Luis Díaz must walk back out onto a football pitch, carrying a fear no goal could heal.
He comes off the bench against Luton. The ninety-fifth minute. The last chance. The ball drops...
And he scores. The whole stadium erupts — but Luis is somewhere else entirely. He lifts his shirt.
Libertad para papá. Freedom for my father. A son, on the biggest stage in the world, begging for the one thing money could never buy.
A nation wept. The world held its breath. And the pressure became impossible to ignore.
Twelve days after he was taken — admitting they had made a terrible mistake — his captors let his father go.
Luis Manuel walked free. The man from the dust came home. And the longest twelve days finally ended.
Today, Luis Díaz is an idol — a star for club and country, the pride of every forgotten village in La Guajira.
But ask him what he treasures, and it was never the trophies. It was a phone call that said: your father is safe.
The skinny boy they overlooked carried his whole people out of the desert — and brought his father home.
